cls: Lipid-modifying nutraceutical - mixture of long-chain aliphatic alcohols (mainly octacosanol) derived from sugar-cane/beeswax
pharm: A natural mixture of higher primary aliphatic alcohols proposed to modulate hepatic cholesterol synthesis and improve LDL receptor processing; marketed as a dietary supplement/over-the-counter lipid-lowering agent in several countries

Usually taken with the evening meal

No established adjustment; use cautiously in liver disease
No specific interaction documented; moderate intake
Lipid profile; bleeding signs if on anticoagulants
summary: Policosanol is a dietary supplement consisting of a mixture of long-chain primary aliphatic alcohols (predominantly octacosanol) obtained from sugar-cane wax or beeswax. It is marketed in parts of Latin America, Asia and Europe as an over-the-counter lipid-lowering and antiplatelet nutraceutical, typically at 5-20 mg once daily with the evening meal. It is NOT an FDA-approved medicine and has no FDA prescribing information; efficacy data are heavily influenced by source/manufacturer, with favourable Cuban studies not consistently reproduced by independent trials. Because it is a supplement, dosing and quality are not standardised. It is generally well tolerated; theoretical concerns include additive bleeding risk with antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs. Pregnancy and lactation safety are not established. Information here is based on EMA/SmPC-style supplement monographs and review literature rather than an FDA label.
indications: Adjunct to lifestyle measures for mild hypercholesterolaemia (supplement use; efficacy disputed)
Marketed for support of cardiovascular/lipid health (nutraceutical claim, not an approved therapeutic indication)

dosage.d: 5 to 20 mg once daily (most studies used 10 mg, some up to 40 mg)
dosage.t: Once daily, usually with the evening meal
dosage.n: Not an approved drug regimen; product strengths vary by brand

admin: Take orally once daily, typically with the evening meal
Use as an adjunct to diet and lifestyle, not a substitute for proven lipid-lowering therapy
Choose a standardised product; potency and purity differ between sugar-cane and beeswax sources
Discuss with a clinician before use if taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs
moa: The proposed mechanism is incompletely defined. Policosanol is thought to down-regulate hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis (acting upstream of HMG-CoA reductase, possibly via AMPK activation and modulation of HMG-CoA reductase expression rather than direct enzyme inhibition) and to enhance LDL-receptor-mediated clearance, thereby lowering LDL cholesterol and modestly raising HDL. Antiplatelet effects (reduced platelet aggregation and thromboxane generation) have also been reported. The clinical relevance of these mechanisms is uncertain because independent trials have frequently failed to confirm the large lipid effects seen in early manufacturer-sponsored studies.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to policosanol or to its source material (sugar-cane wax or beeswax)
relative: Active bleeding or use of antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy (theoretical additive bleeding risk)
Reliance on it in place of evidence-based lipid therapy in high cardiovascular risk patients
monitor: Fasting lipid profile to assess any response
Signs of bleeding or bruising if combined with antithrombotic drugs

preg: There are no adequate data on policosanol use in pregnancy. As a supplement of uncertain benefit, it should be avoided during pregnancy unless advised otherwise by a clinician.
lact: It is not known whether policosanol or its components are excreted in human milk. Because of insufficient safety data, avoid use while breastfeeding.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment has been established and pharmacokinetic data in renal impairment are lacking; use with general caution.
hepatic: Policosanol is thought to act on the liver; specific data in hepatic impairment are lacking. Use cautiously in patients with liver disease and monitor as clinically indicated.

moderate: Antiplatelet agents (e.g. aspirin, clopidogrel) - possible additive inhibition of platelet aggregation and bleeding risk
Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, DOACs) - theoretical increased bleeding risk
minor: Other lipid-lowering supplements - additive but unpredictable lipid effects
interactions.food: Commonly taken with the evening meal; no specific food interaction documented
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction documented; advise moderation as part of cardiovascular lifestyle measures
interactions.diagnostics: May lower LDL and total cholesterol on lipid panels; interpret lipid results in context

common: Generally well tolerated; mild gastrointestinal upset
serious: No well-documented serious adverse effects at usual doses
rare: Increased bleeding tendency when combined with antithrombotic drugs (theoretical)
emergency: Allergic reaction with rash, swelling or breathing difficulty (seek urgent care)

monitoring: Fasting lipid profile before and during use to judge benefit
Bleeding/bruising if taken with antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs
Reassessment of cardiovascular risk and whether proven therapy is needed
counsel: This is a dietary supplement, not an FDA-approved medicine, and its cholesterol-lowering benefit is uncertain
Do not use it as a replacement for prescribed statins or other proven heart-protective treatment
Continue a healthy diet, exercise and other lifestyle measures
Tell your doctor if you take blood thinners or aspirin, as there is a possible added bleeding risk
Avoid during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless your clinician advises otherwise
pk: Lipid changes, if any, develop gradually over weeks of regular use
Poorly characterised in humans; limited human pharmacokinetic data
Effects depend on continued daily intake
Store in a cool, dry place away from light, per product label
pearls: NOTE: Policosanol is NOT FDA-approved and has no FDA prescribing information; this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC-style and review-literature data for a dietary supplement
Large lipid-lowering effects reported in early Cuban manufacturer studies have generally NOT been reproduced by independent trials
Product source (sugar-cane wax vs beeswax) and standardisation vary widely, affecting any potential effect
Should not replace proven lipid-lowering therapy in patients at significant cardiovascular risk
Possible additive bleeding risk with antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs - counsel patients accordingly
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses together. Missing an occasional dose of this supplement is not harmful.
overdose: There is no specific data on policosanol overdose and no specific antidote. Toxicity is expected to be low; manage any ingestion of a large amount supportively and seek medical advice. Watch for gastrointestinal upset and, if combined with antithrombotic drugs, signs of bleeding.
